newsitem.title: UK: Domestic investors to shield French bonds.
newsitem.headline: Domestic investors to shield French bonds.

text.p: Weighty domestic investment should allow French bonds to continue to overlook issues that normally make bond markets flinch -- swelling deficits, job creation schemes and rising wages, analysts said on Wednesday.
Foreign investors will probably not like what they hear on those issues when Prime Minister Lionel Jospin delivers a key speech on Thursday but domestic players should carry them through.
"I don't see any reason to get too negative here," Steve Major, head of bond research at Credit Lyonnais in London. "The OAT/Bund spread at 10 under is logical."

Optimism over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) has kept the yield on 10-year OAT bonds trading in a tight range of around 15 basis points (0.15 percentage point) above and 15 under comparable German Bunds since about May 1996.
Even the transition to a left-wing government from a centre-right one on June 1 and the recent turmoil over currency union has failed to move the gap.

But the market faces a crucial test on Thursday with Jospin's debut parliamentary speech. He will have to walk a fine line between delivering election promises of more jobs and adhering to strict fiscal requirements of EMU.
Economists believe he will reaffirm his election pledge to push for a shorter working week and to create 700,000 jobs in three years.

He may also predict the deficit will overshoot the 3.0 percent of gross domestic product target required by EMU and could signal he supports a reopening of public sector wage negotiations. He could also address clamours for a rise in the minimum wage.

But with the bulk of the French market held by domestic players, OATs should be able to ride out any turbulence caused by Jospin's comments, said Adrian Owens, European economist at Bank Julius Baer in London.

Favourable tax treatment encourages life assurance companies and funds to buy bonds over equities, a system which the government is unlikely to change until after candidates are chosen for EMU in the spring 1998.
"I think (the OAT/Bund gap) is going to be around about those levels until we see some change in the tax system in France," Owens said.
Major at Credit Lyonnais was not so sure Jospin would undermine the market anyway, noting France walked away from the Amsterdam summit with only paper promises on job creation.
"All the evidence so far is that the French government is gradually adjusting its position from one which radically departed from the previous one to one that looks very much the same," he said.
"People are already frustrated that these promises are not being fulfilled."
However, Julian Jessop, European economist at Nikko Europe in London, was not so sure the market would stand firm.
"What often happens is that markets initially over-react then they become complacent again. I think we're approaching that third stage when some of the concerns are reignited," he said.
"I think it's a time for heading back to the safe havens -- Germany, the U.S. and the U.K.," he said. "Even for domestic investors there are concerns that could be triggered tomorrow."

Both Owens and Jessop said yields of more peripheral EMU countries like Italy and Spain would be more vulnerable to widening against Bunds on Thursday if Jospin suggested that he was not 100 percent committed to EMU.
